findings.title: Gate-versus-enumeration check cannot see the sign of d: a gate that scores baseline minus candidate passes the full bench
findings.claim: The only bench check that goes through decide_suite uses a symmetric 1-cell law (1/3,1/3,1/3) and a 2-cell pair of mirror-image laws ((1/2,1/3,1/6),(1/6,1/3,1/2)). Flipping d for every pair turns that pair into the same set of laws with the cells swapped. The wealth depends only on the cumulative counts, so the distribution at every round end is unchanged. A gate that scores the pair difference with the wrong sign therefore matches operating_characteristics exactly. The 'gate and enumeration agree' check (brief item 4) cannot detect a reversed scoring direction, which is the most basic gate defect.

findings.title: Rational has no size bound: manifest validity depends on an interpreter setting, and float-derived rule values are accepted
findings.claim: The Rational pattern `^[1-9][0-9]*/[1-9][0-9]*$` allows any number of digits. Three consequences, all fixable only before the freeze. (1) parse_rational calls Fraction(text), which is subject to CPython's int-string digit limit (default 4300, changed by PYTHONINTMAXSTRDIGITS or sys.set_int_max_str_digits). The same stored manifest is valid under one interpreter configuration and a ValidationError under another, which contradicts 'same inputs, same sealed decision, on every platform'. The trigger is exotic. (2) The schema accepts float-derived values such as format_rational(Fraction(0.1)) = 3602879701896397/36028797018963968, so a phase 2 descriptor that converts a YAML float naively seals a rule that is not 1/10 and nothing refuses it. (3) Exact-arithmetic cost grows with digit count: a schema-valid manifest can make the plan check and the gate take minutes.
findings.evidence: probe6.py: a manifest with a 4301-digit stake denominator written under PYTHONINTMAXSTRDIGITS=0 seals and reloads with a valid seal; the same file under the default setting gives 'load failed: ValidationError'. probe3.py under the default: 4300 digits accepted, 4301 gives 'Value error, Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string conversion'; under PYTHONINTMAXSTRDIGITS=0 both 4301 and 6000 are accepted. Inline run: delta=3602879701896397/36028797018963968 with alpha=3602879701896397/72057594037927936 is accepted and check_suite_plan returns (). probe5.py (1000 cells x 100 rounds, one stake near 1/4): 3-digit rationals check_suite_plan 1.39 s and decide_suite with no trials 6.08 s; 20-digit 37.25 s and 20.69 s; 60-digit check_suite_plan 119.33 s and decide_suite did not finish inside the 150 s limit.
findings.fix: Before the freeze, bound the digits in both the pattern and parse_rational, for example `^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}/[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$` (alpha >= 1/1000000 still fits). Update contract section 2 and add acceptance cases for a 10-digit part and for format_rational(Fraction(0.1)). After the freeze this cannot change without a re-freeze.

findings.title: Every seed derives from the whole rule digest: 'fixed' scenarios change with candidate_id, prior_runs, budgets or any label, and no sealed field can hold them constant
findings.claim: cell_seed is keyed by suite_rule_sha256, which covers every manifest field except experiment_id, created_at and record_sha256. So in scenario_seeds='fixed' a cell's scenario is fixed only inside one experiment. A new candidate_id (every commit in CI), an added prior_runs entry, or a changed label or budget re-draws every cell's seed. This follows ADR 0011 item 7 as written, but the consequence is not stated anywhere, and v1's explicit base_seed has no counterpart: the same scenario set cannot be reused across candidates, an empty commit re-rolls all scenarios without any visible seed change in the manifest diff, and a 'seed collision' (about N^2/2^54, 5.5e-7 at 100,000 cells) can only be escaped by editing sealed content. A seed input or salt field cannot be added after the freeze.
findings.evidence: probe4.py, one-cell manifest, fixed mode: seed 6559476885443160; identical manifest with candidate.candidate_id='sha2': 7516129318952942; identical manifest with prior_runs=(first experiment_id,): 8170983314806745.
findings.fix: Decide before the freeze. Either accept it and state it in docs/STATISTICS_SUITE.md and the report text ('fixed' means fixed across rounds of one experiment; a new candidate or rerun draws new scenarios), or key the seed on a narrower sealed digest (suite_id, sorted tasks, conditions, toolset or mcp_server, seed_derivation, plus an optional sealed salt) while keeping the full rule digest in experiment_id.

findings.title: Contract and budgets are suite-wide; a task cannot carry its own hard invariants or limits
findings.claim: SuiteTask holds only task_id and task. ContractSpec.required_tools, forbidden_tools, max_tool_calls and max_calls_per_tool, and Budgets, apply to every cell, and one candidate hard violation BLOCKs the suite. On a suite with different kinds of task, required_tools can list only tools every task must call, and the budget must fit the hardest task. Per-task success logic is expressible, because the single oracle receives the task (verified: run_trial takes the contract as a separate argument and the oracle is called with spec.task). A per-task override cannot be added later: digest_payload hashes every declared field, so even an optional new field changes every archived digest.
findings.evidence: File read: SuiteTask fields at suite_schema.py:52-54; run_trial(spec, emit_event, contract) at runner.py:1453-1476; build_suite_round passes budgets=manifest.budgets to every spec (suite_schedule.py:112). No script needed.
findings.fix: Confirm this is intended before the freeze (PLAN.md says 'one check function', which the oracle covers). If per-task invariants or budgets are wanted in v2.x, add optional `contract_overrides` or `budgets` to SuiteTask now; otherwise record it in DECISIONS.md D-03 as a design exclusion next to task weights.

findings.title: Run directory named by the raw experiment_id: Windows device names and path length
findings.claim: The directory name is `<suite_id>@<64 hex>`, up to 129 characters. That is fine on macOS and Linux (NAME_MAX 255) and as a Windows path component, and '@' is legal on all three. Two Windows risks remain. A suite_id with a reserved device name before its first dot ('con.v1', 'NUL.suite', 'com1.x') gives a reserved directory name. findings.title: Rational strings have no digit bound: a valid sealed manifest drives every decision into the 'gate computation failed' guard, and a 5 KB manifest makes decide_suite run for minutes
findings.claim: Rational is `^[1-9][0-9]*/[1-9][0-9]*$` with no length limit. (a) An alpha whose denominator d has exactly 4300 digits parses (int/str limit is 4300 digits), the manifest constructs, seals, and passes check_suite_plan, but `format_rational(2 / alpha)` in `_fields` needs str() of a 4301-digit integer and raises. Every `_decision(rebuilt, ...)` call then falls to the last-resort template, so decide_suite returns ERROR ('gate computation failed') with manifest_sha256 == '' and trials_sha256 == '' for a store that evaluate_rounds scores as PASS. Contract section 7 says no valid input is known to reach that guard; this one does. (b) Long-digit stakes/delta make exact Fraction powers explode: a schema-valid manifest of a few KB turns decide_suite on the default-size plan into a multi-minute computation. Rated blocking only because the bound belongs in suite_schema.py, which freezes after phase 1; no wrong PASS/BLOCK results from it.

findings.title: trials_sha256 is taken from un-normalised supplied seals: a bytes seal yields a sealed, replayable PASS whose trials_sha256 is empty
findings.where: /Users/ajay/Developer/.arci-worktrees/wt-v2-suite/src/arci/suite_gate.py:29-40 (_digest/_safe_digest), :236 (digest computed before and outside normalisation), :317 (PASS built with that digest); contract section 5 'Fields of every decision', trials_sha256 bullet
findings.claim: Every check and the verdict use the rebuilt trials, but the top-level trials_sha256 is computed from the supplied instances. Pydantic lax mode coerces bytes/bytearray to str on rebuild, so a trial copied with `record_sha256=<same hex as bytes>` passes checks 5, 6, 7 and 8, while `_safe_digest` sees a non-str and returns ''. decide_suite then returns PASS (or BLOCK) with trials_sha256 == '' and a non-empty history[-1].trials_sha256, and replay_suite_decision confirms it. The decision is not bound to its evidence and differs from the decision for the identical store with str seals. v1's gate fails closed on the same input. A str subclass with an overridden __lt__ gives a PASS with a non-canonical trials_sha256, and if that __lt__ raises a BaseException it escapes decide_suite (v1 catches BaseException). The implementation follows the contract's letter ('taken from the supplied instances ... "" if any supplied record_sha256 is not a str'); the contract did not anticipate that such a store can pass every check.

findings.title: decide_suite cost is superlinear in rounds: about 10 hours for a valid 1-cell x 100,000-round store that stays INCONCLUSIVE
findings.where: /Users/ajay/Developer/.arci-worktrees/wt-v2-suite/src/arci/suite_gate.py:115 (scored_wealth recomputed from scratch each round) and :122 (_digest re-sorts and re-hashes all trials seen so far each round); suite_stats.py:87-95
findings.claim: evaluate_rounds recomputes, at every round end, exact Fraction powers over the cumulative counts and a sorted hash over all cumulative seals. Per-look cost grows faster than linearly in cumulative pairs, so total cost over R looks is roughly cubic for the wealth and quadratic for the digest. A wide store is cheap (one look); a many-round store that never crosses (trivial to build: alternate +1/-1 pairs, both wealths decay) is not. The cumulative per-round digest is quadratic by its contract definition (about N*R^2*67 bytes hashed: ~670 GB for 1 cell x 100,000 rounds), so the gate alone cannot fix that part. A runner that calls evaluate_rounds on the whole store after every round, as section 5 describes, pays the sum of these costs again per round.
findings.evidence: a4_cost.py (full decide_suite, INCONCLUSIVE at every round): `N=1 R=1000 decide_suite=1.28s`, `N=1 R=4000 decide_suite=9.71s`, `N=1 R=8000 pairs=8000 decide_suite=54.79s hist=8000`, `N=20 R=500 pairs=10000 decide_suite=5.01s`. cProfile at R=4000: 26.7 of 28.8 s in evaluate_rounds, 17.7 s in _digest, 8.4 s in scored_wealth. a5_micro.py, cost of one look at n cumulative pairs: `n=8000 digest=6.20ms scored_wealth=10.02ms`, `n=32000 digest=37.76ms scored_wealth=95.59ms`, `n=100000 digest=116.37ms scored_wealth=891.19ms total=1009.71ms`; `trapezoid integral of per-look cost over 100,000 one-cell looks: 36740 s = 10.21 h` (the same integral to n=8000 gives 55 s, matching the measured 54.79 s). For 20 cells x 5,000 rounds the same integral divided by 20 gives about 0.5 h. For contrast a9_wide.py: `N=100000 R=1 pairs=100000 decide_suite=16.8s maxrss=2341MiB`.
findings.fix: Keep per-stake integer wealth numerators over a fixed common denominator and multiply them forward by each round's counts instead of recomputing powers (the _integer_wealth approach already in suite_stats.py). For the digest, change the contract's round digest to a chain (hash of the previous round digest plus this round's sorted seals), or cap max_rounds in the schema before it freezes. Give the runner an incremental entry point rather than a full re-walk per round.

findings.title: evaluate_rounds decides round completeness by envelope count, and reads outcomes without normalising
findings.where: /Users/ajay/Developer/.arci-worktrees/wt-v2-suite/src/arci/suite_gate.py:107-113 (completeness test and pairing), :63-73 (`is Outcome.X` on raw values)
findings.claim: A round is treated as complete when it holds exactly 2*n_cells envelopes, whatever their ids. With a duplicated envelope and a missing one (a retry appended to the store) it returns a look, possibly PASS, for an incomplete round: `pairs=20` while the counts sum to 19, or one pair counted twice. A round with one envelope too many is silently treated as a trailing partial round, so a runner that asks 'run another round?' sees INCONCLUSIVE at the previous round forever and no error. On envelopes holding plain-string outcomes (model_copy/model_construct) it does not count 'ERROR' as errored and counts 'PASS' as not passed, so it disagrees with decide_suite on the same input. decide_suite itself fails closed in all these cases; the contract leaves evaluate_rounds unspecified outside its assumptions, so this is a risk for the phase-2 runner, not a contract breach.
findings.evidence: a8_rounds.py: `round1: last pair baseline missing, candidate twice: [(1, 'PASS', 20, (0, 0, 19, 0), 0)]`; `same with +1 outcomes -> looks like a full round: [(1, 'PASS', 20, (0, 0, 20, 0), 0)]` while `decide_suite on that store: verdict=ERROR ... ('trial schedule mismatch',)`; `2 errored pairs (tol 1) with outcome as plain str: [(1, 'INCONCLUSIVE', 20, (0, 20, 0, 0), 0)]` while `decide_suite: verdict=ERROR ... ('errored pairs exceed max_errored_pairs',)`. a1_types.py: `evaluate_rounds raw, all outcomes plain strings: [('INCONCLUSIVE', {'minus': 0, 'zero': 20, 'plus': 0, 'errored': 0})]` against decide_suite PASS. a12_misc.py: `evaluate_rounds: r1 complete, r2 complete + 1 duplicate envelope (41 in round 2): [(1, 'INCONCLUSIVE')]` against `r1, r2 complete: [(1, 'INCONCLUSIVE'), (2, 'INCONCLUSIVE')]`. A genuine trailing partial round behaves as specified (`round1 complete + 39 of round2: [(1, 'INCONCLUSIVE', ...)]`, including when the partial round holds a candidate hard violation).
findings.fix: Define a complete round as: the distinct trial ids of the round equal the scheduled ids for that round. Raise ValueError on a duplicate id or on more than 2*n_cells envelopes in a round instead of treating it as partial. Either normalise envelopes inside evaluate_rounds or state in the contract that the runner must pass validated instances.

findings.title: Gate scores on `outcome` alone: envelopes that contradict themselves are accepted as PASS evidence
findings.claim: With a correct spec hash and seal, a candidate envelope counts as PASS even when termination is harness_error, grader_error or replay_miss, when contract.grader_error is set and contract.success is False, or when it has no contract result at all. `variant` is not compared with the spec, so an envelope labelled with the other arm's variant is accepted, and events carrying another trial's trial_id are accepted (a round cloned into later rounds under the scheduled spec hashes passes). This matches the eight checks as written and v1's gate.py:41-50, and seals are not signatures, so none of it defeats a deliberate forger. It matters more in v2 because errored pairs are now tolerated and scored, so the ERROR/FAIL/PASS label of a harness failure changes the verdict.
findings.evidence: a2_manifest.py: `termination=harness_error but outcome PASS(cand)/FAIL(base): verdict=PASS exit=0 stop=1`; `contract.grader_error set + success False, candidate outcome PASS: verdict=PASS`; `termination=replay_miss, outcome PASS/FAIL, scheduled hash: verdict=PASS`; `swap arms, scheduled spec hash, variant label left as other arm: verdict=PASS` with `variant on a 'candidate' trial: base`; `round1 cloned into 2..4 with scheduled spec hash; events still say round 1: verdict=PASS ... stop=4` with `event trial_id of a round-4 trial: r000001:t19:clean:candidate vs trial_id r000004:t19:clean:candidate`. Envelopes of genuine REPLAY-mode or LIVE-mode specs are rejected (`trial schedule mismatch`).
findings.fix: If cheap consistency is wanted, add to check 6 (or a new named check): variant equals the spec's variant; outcome is ERROR exactly when termination is harness_error/grader_error/replay_miss or contract.grader_error is set; every event's trial_id equals the envelope's. Otherwise record in the trust notes that the suite gate trusts `outcome` as written.

findings.title: Checks 1 and 5 (canonical_json of the JSON-mode dump) reject valid-seal trials over volatile fields and miss unencodable dict keys
findings.claim: (a) A non-finite float in a VOLATILE field (usage.wall_seconds, Event.at_ms) leaves the trial's seal valid and its record_sha256 unchanged, but check 5 fails. Two stores with the same manifest_sha256 and the same trials_sha256 therefore get different decisions (PASS and ERROR), so the decision is not a function of the digests it reports. (b) Pydantic's JSON-mode dump replaces a lone surrogate in a dict KEY with U+FFFD, so check 1/5 does not see it; the record is then reported as 'manifest seal invalid', 'suite rule digest mismatch', 'trial schedule mismatch' (or 'trial seal invalid') instead of the 'values invalid' reason the contract intends, and the manifest case uses the mirrored fields rather than the fixed template. Both fail closed; no PASS or BLOCK is reachable this way.
findings.evidence: a6_strings.py: `usage.wall_seconds=inf: verdict=ERROR ... reasons=('trial values invalid',)` with `seal still valid: True same record_sha256: True` and `decision equals reference: False | same trials_sha256: True | same manifest: True`; same for nan and for `event.at_ms=nan (volatile)`. `final_state key surrogate: verdict=ERROR ... reasons=('trial seal invalid',)`. a7_key.py: `python-mode key: ["'\\ud800'"]`, `json-mode key: ["'\\ufffd\\ufffd\\ufffd'"]`, `canonical_json ok: 725`; `manifest task KEY surrogate: verdict=ERROR ... reasons=('manifest seal invalid', 'suite rule digest mismatch', 'trial schedule mismatch') ... msha=13d852ce`. Surrogates in string values and in every string field are caught as specified, and results were identical under PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and 123.
findings.fix: Run the encodability test on `digest_payload(record)` (what the seal actually covers, keys included) instead of, or in addition to, the JSON-mode dump; decide in the contract whether non-finite volatile floats should fail a trial.

findings.title: replay_suite_decision accepts a decision whose verdict is a plain string
findings.claim: The decision argument is not normalised. A SuiteDecision copied with `verdict='PASS'` (str, not Verdict) has a valid seal and compares equal to the recomputed decision because StrEnum equals its value, so replay returns True for a record on which `decision.verdict is Verdict.PASS` is False. This is the same look-alike class the contract's 'Normalise first' rule closes for manifests and trials. It follows the contract's literal definition and v1's replay_decision.
findings.evidence: a12_misc.py: `replay_suite_decision(decision with verdict='PASS' str): True | la.verdict is Verdict.PASS: False`. A decision with a changed verdict is rejected (`tampered decision: False`).
findings.fix: Rebuild the decision with SuiteDecision.model_validate(decision.model_dump(mode='python')) before checking its seal and comparing, or have callers read the verdict from the recomputed decision.

findings.title: Wealth uses Fraction arithmetic and is recomputed from scratch every round, so the gate takes minutes at valid registered sizes
findings.where: src/arci/suite_stats.py:87-104 (wealth, scored_wealth); called per round from src/arci/suite_gate.py:115 and from check_suite_plan (suite_stats.py:176-187)
findings.claim: wealth() builds each term as a Fraction product (m**minus * z**zero * p**plus) and adds them up as Fractions. Every multiply and add runs gcd normalisation on numbers with millions of bits, so the cost grows with the square of the pair count. scored_wealth() calls wealth() twice, and each call computes both directions, so half the work is thrown away. evaluate_rounds then recomputes this from scratch for every cumulative round, which makes a long run cost about the cube of the number of rounds. The results stay exact and deterministic. The problem is speed: manifests that the schema accepts become impractical to decide or replay. The contract says wealth(0, 100_000, 0, rule) must return promptly, and with a multi-stake rule it does not.
findings.evidence: Measured on this Mac (M-series). Scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ajay--claude-spares-spare-8K9guD/39ca2335-7a5a-47d9-a374-69d92a47e1d0/scratchpad/p1review/. (a) bignum.py, run on 3.13 (output in bignum313.txt): one wealth() call at 100,000 pairs takes 0.52 to 0.95 s with the default rule. With a valid rule of 8 stakes k/1009, delta 1/997 and alpha 1/1000000 it takes 63.45 s at (0,100000,0), 29.21 s at (100000,0,0), 30.86 s at (0,0,100000) and 65.92 s at (33333,33333,33334). (b) wealth_cmp.py runs the same rule at n=20000: wealth plus crossed takes 2.35, 2.24, 2.39 and 2.20 s on 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. An integer evaluation of the same crossing, using one common denominator and no gcd, takes about 0.06 s and gives the same answer (same=True). At n=100000 on 3.14 the Fraction path takes 58.96 s and the integer path 0.826 s, again same=True. (c) gate_scale.py repeats evaluate_rounds' per-round work (scored_wealth, crossed, wealth_text, _digest) for a valid default-rule plan of 250 cells by 400 rounds (100,000 pairs), with evidence exactly on the margin (mean d = -delta) so no test crosses. That costs 220.1 s of wealth plus 9.5 s of digest per decide_suite call (gate_scale.txt), and replay_suite_decision does it all again. For 10 cells by 2000 rounds (20,000 pairs) it costs 60.0 s, and the wealth part grows about as rounds cubed. (d) For the 8-stake rule at 100,000 registered pairs, check_suite_plan alone needs at least one wealth(0,100000,0) call plus scored_wealth(0,0,N-E,E), which is two more wealth calls. From (a), that is roughly 2 to 3 minutes before any trial is read.
findings.fix: Evaluate the crossing in integers, as _integer_wealth already does for operating_characteristics. Use one common denominator D per direction and numerator = sum over stakes of a**minus * b**zero * c**plus, then compare numerator * alpha.numerator with 2 * alpha.denominator * len(stakes) * D**n. Build the Fraction only for wealth_text, or have wealth_text take numerator and denominator directly. In scored_wealth, compute only the direction it keeps. In evaluate_rounds, carry each stake's per-direction integer powers across rounds (multiply in the increments) rather than recomputing. Add a timing test with 8 odd-denominator stakes at SUITE_MAX_PAIRS, not just the default rule. Outputs (crossed flags, wealth_text, record_sha256) are unchanged by this, so it can land without touching any frozen file.

findings.title: Stationarity assumption omits a breaker the schedule itself introduces: the per-round arm-order flip
findings.claim: The proof needs each cell to have the same law in every round (or, failing that, every single round's suite mean to obey the null). The doc lists model updates, provider drift, changing conditions and scenario selection as breakers, and says fixed seeds remove seed changes as a cause. It does not say that arm_order() hashes the real round in both seed modes, so which arm runs first in a given cell changes from round to round by construction. If execution order has any effect on success (warm caches, rate limits, a local model server's state), a cell's law in fixed mode is not stationary and the per-round means differ deterministically with the hash. The fixed-mode claim then silently reduces to the unverified per-round condition, with the same 'bound holds only on average over the draw' weakness ADR 0011 item 3 rejected sampled cells for. The order-averaged Delta a user would naturally read as the estimand is not protected.
findings.evidence: Script /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ajay--claude-spares-spare-8K9guD/39ca2335-7a5a-47d9-a374-69d92a47e1d0/scratchpad/p1review/misc.py: defaults, two-point laws, order-averaged suite mean exactly -delta, cell mean -delta+e when the candidate runs second and -delta-e when first, 120 random order patterns per case (crossings exact via suite_stats.wealth/crossed, path probabilities in floats). N=1, R=400: e=0.05 gives false PASS max 2.77% and false BLOCK max 2.86%, 5% of patterns above 2.5%; e=0.10 gives false PASS max 3.66%, false BLOCK max 3.54%, 22-23% of patterns above 2.5%. N=5, R=80, e=0.10: false BLOCK max 3.20% (4% of patterns above 2.5%). N=20, R=20: no pattern above 2.5% up to e=0.10 (max 1.92%). With e=0.02 nothing exceeded 2.5% on any grid. So the exposure is real but needs an order effect of about 5 points and a small grid.
findings.fix: Add one sentence to the 'same null in every round' bullet and to the Scenario seeds section: arm order is re-drawn per round by hash in both modes; if order affects outcomes, per-cell laws are not stationary and the guarantee holds only under the per-round condition (every round's suite mean, with that round's arm orders, obeys the null). State that Delta_c is defined for the registered order of that round, or assume explicitly that order has no effect on success.

findings.title: Common-mode limit is stated without the magnitude ADR 0011 item 6 attaches to it, and nothing in the bench measures it
findings.claim: ADR 0011 item 6 states the common-mode assumption together with its failure size ('with 20 cells, a whole round sharing one outcome takes false PASS from 0.9% to 67%'). The doc keeps the qualitative statement ('no allowance in the proof', 'not covered by its nominal error budget') but drops the number, and bench/selfcheck_suite.py has no dependent-round case. A reader has no way to tell that the failure is catastrophic rather than a mild inflation.
findings.evidence: Reproduced exactly in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ajay--claude-spares-spare-8K9guD/39ca2335-7a5a-47d9-a374-69d92a47e1d0/scratchpad/p1review/misc.py with suite_stats.wealth/crossed at defaults, N=20, 20 rounds, margin law P(-1)=1/10, P(0)=9/10: independent cells false PASS 0.009034; whole round sharing one outcome false PASS 0.672777 and, on the same margin law, false BLOCK 0.318217 (99.1% of runs give a directional verdict where both nulls hold).

findings.title: Estimand is defined two ways once errors exist, and line 28's E[d] = Delta_c is false for the pairs it names
findings.claim: Line 14 defines success as 'its sealed trial outcome is PASS', under which an ERROR trial is a non-success and Delta_c includes any error-rate asymmetry. Lines 222-230 instead argue through the 'unobserved complete-outcome' process, under which Delta_c is about error-free counterfactual outcomes. These are different population quantities and the doc never says which one PASS/BLOCK speaks about. Separately, lines 27-28 say 'A non-errored pair contributes d ... Linearity gives E[d] = Delta_c': conditional on a pair being non-errored this is false under outcome-dependent missingness, which line 226-227 explicitly allows.
findings.evidence: Counterexample to line 28: a cell where the candidate's latent success rate is 1/2 and the baseline's is 1/2 (Delta_c = 0), and the candidate is marked infrastructure ERROR exactly when it would have failed. Every non-errored pair then has B PASS, so E[d | non-errored] = 1/2, not 0. Check that the bound itself survives both readings: for an errored pair the literal difference [B sealed PASS] - [A sealed PASS] lies in {-1,0,+1}, so scoring -1 in PASS and +1 in BLOCK is dominated by the literal process as well as by any latent completion; scored_wealth agreed with an independent recomputation on 400 random configurations (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ajay--claude-spares-spare-8K9guD/39ca2335-7a5a-47d9-a374-69d92a47e1d0/scratchpad/p1review/indep.py). So this is a gap in the statement, not in error control.
findings.fix: Say that E[d] = Delta_c holds for the complete-outcome difference of every pair, not conditionally on being non-errored, and state that both bounds hold for either reading of Delta_c (ERROR counted as non-success, or the error-free outcome), because worst-case scoring is below both.

findings.title: Bench margin maxima understate what is attainable at defaults; ADR 0011's boundary-maxima row is not reproduced by the bench
findings.claim: The contract asks the bench to reproduce the operating-characteristics rows of ADR 0011.
